storySeeds.title: How heavy stars end, in one Cygnus sweep
storySeeds.summary: Calm supergiant (Deneb) → yellow supergiant in the Milky Way (Sadr) → unstable LBV that erupted in 1600 (P Cyg) → stripped Wolf-Rayet core (WR 136) and the bubble it blew (Crescent, challenge) → the companion of a 21-solar-mass black hole (Cygnus X-1) → a supernova shell (Veil, dark sky). All within ~15° of Sadr.

storySeeds.title: Lyra: seeing double, and doubting it
storySeeds.summary: A single brilliant star (Vega) → a physical quadruple (ε Lyr) → an easy unequal pair (ζ Lyr) → a red giant beside a blue star (δ Lyr) → a pair that swaps gas and eclipses (β Lyr, compare with γ Lyr over nights) → the shell of a dying Sun-like star (M57). Everything sits inside a 6° patch.

storySeeds.title: Near, far and in between: the Summer Triangle as a distance ladder
storySeeds.summary: Altair (17 ly) beside Tarazed (~400 ly) → Vega (25 ly) → faint but close 61 Cygni (11 ly, the first measured distance) → HD 189733 (65 ly) sharing a field with the far more distant Dumbbell → brilliant but remote Deneb (~1,400–2,600 ly). NASA's skywatching notes place M27 inside the Triangle, between Altair and Deneb.

card.question: What does an ordinary star look like in the long, calm prime of its life?
card.glance: The brilliant blue-white star almost overhead on summer evenings, the brightest corner of the Summer Triangle.
card.whyHere: Before a star can look strange, you need a normal one to measure it against, and Vega, bright and close, is the sky's classic yardstick.
card.see: Vega is the jewel of the small constellation Lyra and the first star to appear overhead as the summer sky darkens. In binoculars it becomes a hard white spark ringed by faint stars your eyes alone would miss, with the Double-Double a short hop to the north-east and Lyra's little parallelogram hanging just below.
card.understand: Like the Sun, Vega is a main-sequence star, which simply means it is in the long, steady middle of life, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. It carries a little over twice the Sun's mass, and that extra weight squeezes the core harder, so the fire runs hotter and faster. You can read the result in its color: a surface near 9,500 K glows blue-white.
card.wonder: A disk of dust about a thousand times the Earth–Sun distance across surrounds Vega, and Webb and Hubble found it so smooth that any planets hiding there must be small.
card.connect: Deneb, the Triangle's faintest corner, looks humbler than Vega but lies about a hundred times farther away.
card.answer: It looks like Vega, steady, white and unremarkable in the best sense, though as a heavier star it spends its fuel lavishly and, at about 700 million years, is already well into a life far shorter than the Sun's.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows only a saturated star; the dust disk needs space telescopes and infrared light.
card.notSee: The debris disk, the squashed shape and the temperature difference between pole and equator are all invisible in binoculars.
card.deeper: Hipparcos measured a parallax of 130.23 ± 0.36 mas (25.0 light-years). Vega spins quickly, and we happen to look almost straight down on one pole, which is why its rotation stayed hidden for so long. CHARA interferometry (Monnier et al. 2012) modeled the rotation and found a mass of 2.15 (+0.10/−0.15) solar masses and an age of about 700 (+150/−75) million years, older than earlier estimates. The 2024 Hubble and Webb images (Wolff et al.; Su et al.) show a disk roughly 100 billion miles across with only a subtle gap, ruling out planets larger than Neptune on wide orbits.

teffK.note: pole 8450±140 K, equator 6860±150 K (gravity-darkening-free fit); 7600 K is a representative mean (SIMBAD median 7598 K)

historyHook.text: In 2007 the CHARA telescope array combined light from four telescopes to make a real picture of Altair: a star visibly stretched by its own spin.

card.question: How can a star spin so fast that its own rotation squashes it?
card.glance: The bright white star at the southern corner of the Summer Triangle, with a fainter star on each side.
card.whyHere: Altair is close enough, under 17 light-years, that astronomers have photographed its surface, and the picture showed a star that is the wrong shape.
card.see: Binoculars fit Altair into one field with its two attendants, orange Tarazed about 2° above and fainter Alshain below, a short straight line that marks the eagle, Aquila. Tarazed's warm tint is easy to see, and beside it Altair stays crisp white.
card.understand: Altair is an ordinary adult star, a little heavier and hotter than the Sun, but it turns in a matter of hours where the Sun takes about a month. In 2007 the CHARA array combined the light of four telescopes into one sharp picture, and the star came out visibly stretched, its equator about a quarter wider than its poles. Out at that bulging waist gravity is weaker, so the surface there runs cooler and dimmer.
card.wonder: Its light took under 17 years to reach you, so it left Altair when today's teenagers were being born.
card.connect: Deneb, the Triangle's third corner, is the opposite case: distant, enormous and vastly more powerful.
card.answer: Spin a ball of gas at more than 90% of the speed that would tear it apart and it does what pizza dough does when it is tossed: the middle flings outward. Altair lives in that state, flattened by its own rotation.
card.photoCaption: No licensed photo is bundled; the in-app visuals show its temperature and size beside the Sun.
card.notSee: The flattened shape needs an interferometer with sub-milliarcsecond resolution.
card.deeper: Monnier et al. (2007) imaged Altair with the CHARA Array in the near-infrared. Their best model gives a polar radius of 1.63 and an equatorial radius of 2.03 solar radii, a rotation rate about 92% of break-up, and temperatures from about 8,450 K at the pole to 6,860 K at the equator (gravity darkening). The equator looked even darker than simple models predicted. WIRE satellite photometry showed Altair is also a tiny-amplitude δ Scuti pulsator, varying by under a thousandth of a magnitude (Buzasi et al. 2005).

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.whyHere: A star's brightness in the sky mixes two things, how much light it makes and how far away it is, and Deneb is where the two come apart most dramatically.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.photoCaption: Survey photographs show Deneb buried in Milky Way stars and glowing gas that binoculars render as a rich grainy field.
card.notSee: Its size, light output and distance are all inferred; the point of light looks no bigger than any other star.
card.deeper: Schiller & Przybilla (2008) analyzed a high-resolution spectrum and found Teff 8,525 ± 75 K, log g 1.10, a radius of 203 ± 17 solar radii, about 196,000 solar luminosities and a current mass of 19 ± 3 suns, adopting 802 ± 66 pc from membership of the Cyg OB7 association. Hipparcos (2.31 ± 0.32 mas) points to a much smaller distance, so treat every derived number as uncertain by tens of percent. Its surface is enriched in nitrogen from the core, and the authors favor a star of about 23 solar masses evolving toward the red supergiant stage.

card.question: Can you really read a star's temperature from its color?
card.glance: The swan's head in Cygnus, roughly halfway from Vega to Altair; steady binoculars split it into gold and blue.
card.whyHere: Albireo is the sky's most beautiful color contrast, gold beside blue, and that contrast turns out to be a thermometer you can read from your backyard.
card.see: Albireo marks the head of the swan, at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars on something solid and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark beside it, 34″ away; if the split is hard, let the image drift and watch for the blue point trailing behind.
card.understand: Think of an electric stove ring as it heats: first dull red, then orange, and, if it could get hot enough, white and then blue. Stars are glowing balls of gas and follow the same rule. Their spectra pin down the numbers: the gold star is a cool giant near 4,400 K, the blue one about 13,000 K.
card.wonder: For a century Albireo was the textbook orbiting pair; precise Gaia-era motions now suggest two siblings born together and slowly drifting apart.
card.connect: The Double-Double near Vega shows pairs that truly do orbit each other.
card.answer: You can, and Albireo proves it: the golden star is only about a third as hot as its blue companion, and your eye registers that gap as color. Every tint you notice tonight is a surface temperature read across hundreds of light-years.
card.photoCaption: Wide survey images saturate both stars into one; the colors are best seen live through a steady instrument.
card.notSee: The gold star is itself a close pair (Aa/Ac, 0.3″ apart) that only speckle interferometry resolves.
card.deeper: Drimmel et al. (2021) combined 120 years of radial velocities, speckle astrometry and Hipparcos/Gaia data. Albireo A is a triple-in-a-pair: Aa (K giant, 4,383 K) and Ac orbit every 121.7 (+3.3/−2.9) years, with hints of a fourth body. The A–B pair is "very unlikely" to be bound (bound in at most about 1 in 8 Monte Carlo realizations), yet a chance alignment is improbable (~10⁻⁸), so a common origin about 100 million years ago is favored. The WDS gives 34.3″ at position angle 54° (2025).

card.question: How many stars can hide inside one faint point of light?
card.glance: Two matching white stars about 1.7° north-east of Vega in Lyra; any binoculars split them.
card.whyHere: Many stars that look single are really families, and ε Lyrae is the most elegant demonstration, because every step up in magnification adds to the count.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two matched white stars sit side by side like distant headlights. Very sharp eyes can see them as one slightly stretched star without optics, and any binoculars split them easily.
card.understand: Point a telescope at high power on either star and it splits again, into a pair a couple of arcseconds apart (an arcsecond is a 3,600th of a degree). Both close pairs lie at the same distance, about 158 light-years, and drift across the sky together, which would be a strange coincidence for strangers. Over centuries each pair circles its own balance point, and timing orbits like these is how astronomers weigh stars.
card.wonder: The close pairs are about a hundred times tighter than the wide one, a system within a system.
card.connect: Two degrees south, Sheliak's two stars are packed so tightly they almost touch.
card.answer: Binoculars show two, a telescope shows four, each close pair is surely bound, and their shared distance and motion make a strong case that all four form one system, so the dim point beside Vega is really a small stellar neighborhood.
card.photoCaption: The photo shows the wide pair; resolving the inner pairs needs a telescope and steady air.
card.notSee: The inner pairs, each about 2″ wide, are far below binocular resolution.
card.deeper: The Washington Double Star Catalog lists the wide pair STFA 37 at about 209″ (3.5′) and the inner pair ε¹ (STF 2382 AB) at 2.1″. Gaia EDR3 gives ε¹ A a parallax of 20.69 ± 0.40 mas, about 158 light-years. The wide components share proper motion and distance; whether they are formally bound depends on orbital speeds that are hard to measure for a period this long.

superlatives.claim: prototype of the β Lyrae class of eclipsing binaries

historyHook.text: In 2008 the CHARA array produced the first resolved images of this pair, showing the donor star stretched into a teardrop by its companion.

card.question: Why does Sheliak fade and recover every 13 days, as regular as a clock?
card.glance: The western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra, south of Vega; its brightness changes every few days.
card.whyHere: Some stars change because something passes in front of them, and at Sheliak that something is another star, pressed so close that the two share their gas.
card.see: Sheliak and Sulafat sit 2° apart at the bottom of Lyra, an ideal pair to compare. On some nights they look equal, while at the deepest eclipse Sheliak is clearly the fainter, so note which is brighter and check again a few nights later.
card.understand: We see this pair's orbit almost edge-on, so each star passes in front of the other in turn, an arrangement called an eclipsing binary. The two are so close that the light never settles: the lighter star has been stretched into a teardrop and spills gas onto its partner, which hides inside a thick disk of the stolen material. In 2008 the CHARA array imaged that teardrop directly.
card.wonder: The heavier star, about 13 times the Sun's mass, is completely buried in its disk; we know it is there only by its pull.
card.connect: RR Lyrae, a few degrees away, dims for a different reason: the star itself breathes.
card.answer: Two stars orbiting every 13 days keep stepping in front of each other while one feeds the other. So much gas changes hands that the orbit lengthens by about 19 seconds every year, a clock you can literally watch slowing down.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the light-curve visual shows the typical shape of its brightness changes.
card.notSee: The two stars are far too close for any ordinary telescope to separate; it took an interferometer.
card.deeper: Zhao et al. (2008) imaged the system with CHARA/MIRC at six epochs: the Roche-lobe-filling donor (about 3 solar masses) is tidally distorted, and the roughly 13-solar-mass gainer is hidden in a thick accretion disk. The donor loses about 2 × 10⁻⁵ solar masses per year, lengthening the period by about 19 s per year. VSX lists V = 3.30–4.35 with P = 12.944 d. Gaia EDR3 and Hipparcos parallaxes disagree (3.60 vs 5.26 mas), so the distance is uncertain.

distanceLy.note: Gaia EDR3 3.985 ± 0.027 mas (818 ly); HST/FGS 3.82 ± 0.2 mas (Benedict et al. 2002, ~850 ly)

superlatives.claim: the brightest RR Lyrae star in the sky and the prototype of its class

historyHook.text: Hubble's guidance sensors measured its parallax to calibrate a whole class of cosmic yardsticks used to gauge the distance to other galaxies.

card.question: How can one modest star help measure distances across the Galaxy?
card.glance: An unremarkable 7th–8th magnitude star about 10° from Vega toward Cygnus; you need a chart to pick it out.
card.whyHere: Measuring the Galaxy takes lamps of known power, and this old star from the Milky Way's first generations is the prototype of one of the best.
card.see: RR Lyrae lies about 10° from Vega toward Cygnus and looks like nothing at all, so use the finder chart. Pick two nearby comparison stars and check every half hour: over one evening it can change by a factor of 2.5, rising quickly and sinking slowly.
card.understand: RR Lyrae is an old, low-mass star burning helium in its core, its outer layers swelling and shrinking every 13.6 hours. All such stars shine with nearly the same power, but to learn that power you first need the distance to one of them. In 2002 Hubble's guidance sensors caught the tiny yearly wobble of RR Lyrae itself as Earth orbits the Sun, and the answer came out at about 50 Suns.
card.wonder: It is poor in heavy elements, a visitor from the Galaxy's ancient halo that happens to be passing through our neighborhood.
card.connect: η Aquilae, a young, heavy cousin, pulses once a week and serves as the same kind of yardstick.
card.answer: Once a whole class of stars is known to shine with about 50 Suns, each becomes a measuring stick: catch one pulsing in a distant globular cluster, see how faint it looks, and the shortfall gives its distance.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visual shows the fast rise and slow fall typical of this kind of pulsation.
card.notSee: A slow modulation of its light-curve shape over weeks (the Blazhko effect) needs careful photometry.
card.deeper: Benedict et al. (2002) measured an absolute parallax of 3.82 ± 0.2 mas with HST's Fine Guidance Sensor, giving M_V = 0.61 (+0.10/−0.11) and anchoring the RR Lyrae distance scale (LMC modulus 18.38–18.53). Gaia EDR3 later gave 3.985 ± 0.027 mas. VSX lists V = 7.17–8.14 and P = 0.566775 d with a Blazhko modulation (type RRAB/BL). SIMBAD spectroscopy gives [Fe/H] ≈ −1.4, about 1/25 of the Sun's metal content.

distanceLy.note: Gaia EDR3 1.092 ± 0.028 mas; NASA quotes ~3,000 ly

periodDays.note: orbital period of the red giant + white dwarf pair (VSX 227.5528 d)

superlatives.claim: one of only five known recurrent novae in our galaxy

historyHook.text: It flared to naked-eye brightness in 1866 and again in 1946, then dimmed back for decades; astronomers have been waiting for the next outburst since a tell-tale dip in 2023–24.

eventDependent.note: A new eruption has been expected since 2024. Check AAVSO or recent news before you look: it may be a faint 10th-magnitude star or, briefly, as bright as the crown's stars.

card.question: Why does a faint star in the Northern Crown blaze up every 80 years?
card.glance: Normally a faint star just south-east of the Northern Crown's bowl; in eruption, briefly a new naked-eye star.
card.whyHere: A white dwarf is the Earth-sized ember a Sun-like star leaves behind, and most cool in peace; this one has a neighbor that keeps feeding it.
card.see: Find the semicircle of Corona Borealis, then look about 1° south-east of ε CrB. In quiet times T CrB is a 10th-magnitude speck needing dark skies and the chart; in eruption it climbs to about 2nd magnitude, a new star beside the Crown that fades within about a week.
card.understand: A bloated red giant and a white dwarf circle each other here every 227.6 days, and the dwarf's gravity drags gas off the giant. Hydrogen piles up on the dwarf's surface until the whole layer ignites in a runaway nuclear blast called a nova. It happened in 1866 and again in 1946, and a telltale dip in 2023–24 echoed the one seen before 1946.
card.wonder: The light of any eruption you catch set out around three thousand years ago, so the explosion everyone is waiting for has, in a sense, already happened.
card.connect: Three degrees away, R CrB plays the opposite trick: it fades without warning.
card.answer: Each eruption is the white dwarf flashing off stolen hydrogen, and gathering enough takes about 80 years. The next one is overdue and nobody can name the month, so a bright new star beside the Crown means you are watching it happen.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visual shows the shape of a nova outburst, not a forecast.
card.notSee: The white dwarf and its accretion disk are invisible; even at peak the nova is only a point of light.
card.deeper: GCVS gives a range of 2.0 to 10.8 (recurrent nova, NR); eruptions were recorded in 1866 and 1946, and NASA describes it as one of five recurrent novae known in the Galaxy, about 3,000 light-years away. Gaia EDR3 gives 1.092 ± 0.028 mas. The red giant and white dwarf orbit every 227.6 days (VSX). Pei et al. (2026) traced the 2023–24 "pre-eruption dip" in Swift and AAVSO data as a drop in the accretion rate, a pattern also seen before 1946. Nobody can predict the exact date; NASA's 2024 window passed without an eruption.

teffK.note: two SIMBAD Teff entries since 2000 (7048, 7121 K)

superlatives.claim: prototype of the R Coronae Borealis stars, a class of only a few dozen known members

historyHook.text: Stars of its kind may be the merged remains of two white dwarfs: a gentle cousin of the explosions that destroy such pairs.

eventDependent.note: It can vanish from binocular view for months or years without warning; check AAVSO before you look.

card.question: How can a star vanish from view for months and then come back?
card.glance: At normal light, a 6th-magnitude star inside the Northern Crown's bowl; at other times, missing altogether.
card.whyHere: Most variable stars pulse, eclipse or explode; R Coronae Borealis has a stranger habit, disappearing now and then inside its own soot.
card.see: Look inside the curve of Corona Borealis, about 2° north of δ CrB. At normal light R CrB is an easy binocular star, a little fainter than the Crown's faintest stars; if the spot is empty, the star is in a fade, and that is a real observation too.
card.understand: R CrB is a supergiant, a star swollen to enormous size, and an oddly built one, almost empty of hydrogen and rich in carbon. Now and then a puff of gas leaving its surface cools enough for that carbon to condense into soot, much as a candle flame blackens a cold spoon. When such a cloud forms on our side, the star sinks from 6th magnitude to as faint as 15th.
card.wonder: At its deepest it is thousands of times fainter than normal, as if someone had drawn a curtain across a lamp.
card.connect: Three degrees away, T CrB waits to do the opposite: brighten without warning.
card.answer: It hides behind soot of its own making and stays hidden until the cloud drifts off and thins, which can take months or years. Its strange chemistry hints at an equally strange birth, perhaps two white dwarfs that merged into one swollen star.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visual shows the sudden drop and slow recovery typical of its fades.
card.deeper: R CrB stars are hydrogen-deficient, carbon-rich supergiants that undergo deep, irregular declines when carbon dust condenses in their outflows (Clayton 2012). Two origins are debated: a merger of two white dwarfs, or a final helium-shell flash in a dying star; large amounts of oxygen-18 favor the merger picture, making them low-mass cousins of Type Ia supernova progenitors. About 65 were known in 2012 against thousands predicted. VSX gives V = 5.61 at maximum and 15.1 in deep minimum.

distanceLy.note: parallax 5.9 ± 1.5 mas from the pulsating molecular layer (Lacour et al. 2009); Gaia EDR3 6.27 ± 0.28 mas (~520 ly), but Gaia errors for bright AGB stars are underestimated (Andriantsaralaza et al. 2022)

radiusRsun.note: mean limb-darkened angular radius 12.1 mas with ±2.5 mas pulsation, at 5.9 mas parallax

superlatives.claim: one of the largest brightness ranges of any star visible to the eye at maximum

historyHook.text: Its spectrum shows technetium, an element with no stable form: it must have been forged inside the star recently, by cosmic standards.

eventDependent.note: Its brightness depends on where it is in its ~13-month cycle; check AAVSO for the current phase. Near minimum it is invisible in binoculars.

card.question: How does a dying giant swing from naked-eye bright to invisible?
card.glance: In the swan's neck between Albireo and η Cyg: a red star near maximum, an empty patch near minimum.
card.whyHere: Late in life a star like the Sun breathes in long, deep pulses, and χ Cygni does it more dramatically than almost any other star.
card.see: Sweep from Albireo toward η Cygni along the swan's neck. Near maximum χ Cyg is an obvious orange-red star, while months later the same spot is empty in binoculars. When you compare it with white stars, glance rather than stare, because a long look makes red stars seem brighter.
card.understand: χ Cygni is a giant near the end of its life, so swollen it would swallow the orbit of Mars, and it pulses in and out every 408 days. A pulse alone would change its light only modestly; the drama comes from chemistry. At each low the outer layers cool enough for molecules to form, and these soak up visible light like a fog.
card.wonder: Few stars span a wider range: at maximum you need no optics at all, at minimum you need a good telescope.
card.connect: The Ring Nebula in Lyra shows what such shed gas becomes.
card.answer: Pulsation and chemistry work together, each breath cooling the star's skin until molecules smother its light, so χ Cygni swings by more than ten thousand times. Its spectrum even shows technetium, an element with no stable form, so the star must have forged it recently inside itself.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visual shows a typical Mira cycle, not tonight's phase.
card.deeper: Lacour et al. (2009) imaged χ Cyg with the IOTA interferometer at four phases: the limb-darkened angular radius averages 12.1 mas and swings by 5.1 mas, a diameter change of up to 40%. Tracking a molecular layer falling back onto the star gave a parallax of 5.9 ± 1.5 mas and a mass of 2.1 (+1.5/−0.7) solar masses. It is an S-type star, between ordinary oxygen-rich giants and carbon stars; technetium in its spectrum (ApJ 310, 371, 1986) proves fresh dredge-up from its interior. VSX range: V 3.3–14.2, P = 408.05 d.

massMsun.note: O-supergiant donor 40.6 +7.7/-7.1 Msun; its black-hole companion 21.2 ± 2.2 Msun

superlatives.claim: a star you can see in binoculars that orbits a black hole
superlatives.scope: one of the very few such systems within binocular reach

historyHook.text: Cygnus X-1 was the first X-ray source widely accepted as a black hole; in 2021 radio astrometry re-weighed it at about 21 Suns.

card.question: Can you see a star that is orbiting a black hole?
card.glance: A 9th-magnitude star half a degree from η Cygni in the swan's neck: unremarkable, unforgettable once you know.
card.whyHere: Most heavy stars end their lives out of sight, but here in the swan's neck is one of the first places where astronomers became sure black holes are real.
card.see: Center η Cygni, midway along the swan's neck. About 0.4° to the east-north-east, less than a Moon's width away, a 9th-magnitude star slightly brighter than its neighbors is the visible star of Cygnus X-1, and nothing about it looks special.
card.understand: This blue supergiant, about 40 times the Sun's mass, whips around an unseen partner every 5.6 days. Weighing the partner uses the same trick as weighing planets: measure how fast and how far the visible star swings to and fro, and gravity tells you what must be pulling it. In 2021 radio measurements pinned down the distance, and the partner came out at about 21 Suns while giving off no starlight at all.
card.wonder: The light you see set off over seven thousand years ago, before writing was invented.
card.connect: The Veil Nebula shows the other way a heavy star can end: blown apart.
card.answer: You are looking at one. An object that heavy which gives off no light of its own can only be a black hole, the collapsed core of a massive star, and gas torn from the supergiant glows in X-rays as it spirals in.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled: any picture of the black hole and its disk is an artist's illustration, not a photograph.
card.notSee: The black hole, its accretion disk and its jets are detected only in X-rays and radio.
card.deeper: Miller-Jones et al. (2021) used VLBA radio astrometry to measure a distance of 2.22 (+0.18/−0.17) kpc. Refitting the orbit gave a black hole of 21.2 ± 2.2 solar masses and an O9.7 Iab donor of 40.6 (+7.7/−7.1), with a spin parameter above 0.9985 (3σ, aligned spin). These masses, larger than earlier values (Chandra quoted 14.8 Suns at 6,070 ly in 2011), imply that massive stars in our Galaxy lose less mass in winds than once thought. The donor varies slightly (ellipsoidal) with the 5.6-day orbit (GCVS).

distanceLy.note: 1.61 ± 0.18 kpc from intensity interferometry + atmosphere models; agrees with Gaia

superlatives.claim: gave its name to the "P Cygni profile", the spectral signature of a star blowing a wind

historyHook.text: In 1600 a "new star" appeared here at third magnitude; the shell of gas it threw off is still expanding around the star.

eventDependent.note: A luminous blue variable: it has been near 5th magnitude for centuries but can flare; we never state its current brightness.

card.question: What happens when a star is almost too heavy to hold itself together?
card.glance: A modest 5th-magnitude star about 2½° south-west of Sadr, the center of the Northern Cross in Cygnus.
card.whyHere: The heaviest stars live on a knife edge, and in 1600 this one slipped, flaring up as a new third-magnitude star where none had been noticed before.
card.see: From Sadr, at the center of the Northern Cross, slide about 2½° south-west toward Albireo. P Cygni is a plain white point against the Milky Way, easy in binoculars, and nothing in the view hints at its power.
card.understand: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable, one of the heaviest and most luminous kinds of star. In a star this bright the outflowing light itself pushes on the gas almost as hard as gravity pulls it back, so the outer layers are barely held. It leaks mass in a fierce wind and now and then lets go of much more at once; the 1600 eruption threw off a shell that is still expanding today.
card.wonder: It still looks this bright from over five thousand light-years away.
card.connect: WR 136, just over a degree away, has already blown off its outer layers.
card.answer: It starts to come apart: light nearly overpowers gravity, and the star sheds itself in a steady wind and sudden outbursts like the one of 1600. Its name lives on in the P Cygni profile, the spectral signature astronomers use to spot any star blowing a wind.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the 10″ nebula of the 1600 outburst shows only in infrared spectra.
card.notSee: The expanding shell from the 1600 eruption is a few arcseconds across and needs infrared spectroscopy.
card.deeper: The 1600 AD outburst left a nebula about 10″ across, with a total mass of about 0.1 solar mass, mostly ionized and glowing in [Fe II] (Smith & Hartigan 2006). Kashi (2010) suggested the 17th-century peaks were triggered by a companion at periastron. De Almeida et al. (2022) measured 1.61 ± 0.18 kpc by combining intensity interferometry with models, agreeing with Gaia. GCVS lists it as an S Dor variable with a historical range of 3.0–6.0.

teffK.note: stellar temperature 70,000–110,000 K; ~70,000 K best fits star and nebula together

historyHook.text: Infrared images show the Crescent Nebula around it is made almost entirely of gas the star itself threw off, with hardly any swept-up interstellar material.

card.question: What is left when a heavy star blows away its outer layers?
card.glance: A 7½-magnitude star 2.7° south-west of Sadr in Cygnus, at the center of the Crescent Nebula.
card.whyHere: Follow a heavy star past P Cygni's unstable stage and you reach this one, which has already lost its envelope and sits inside a bubble of its own making.
card.see: From Sadr, drift about 2.7° south-west with the chart to a plain white point among the Milky Way stars. The Crescent Nebula around it challenges even big binoculars under dark skies, and a nebula filter helps; most observers see only the star, which is still worth the hop.
card.understand: WR 136 is a Wolf-Rayet star, a heavyweight that lost its hydrogen envelope, first as a bloated red supergiant and then through a fierce wind, leaving its hot interior exposed at around 70,000 K. That fast wind is now plowing into the slower gas shed earlier and piling it into a shell. Infrared images show the Crescent is made almost entirely of the star's own cast-off material, with hardly any swept-up interstellar gas.
card.wonder: The Crescent around it holds roughly 25 solar masses of gas, almost all of it once part of this one star.
card.connect: Cygnus X-1 shows what such a collapse can leave behind: a black hole.
card.answer: A bare, scorching core, still shining, inside a shell made from its own former outer layers. Wolf-Rayet stars live the last, brief chapter of a heavy star's life, and this one is probably not far from collapsing altogether.
card.photoCaption: Deep photos show the Crescent Nebula's glowing filaments; in binoculars the star is a point and the nebula at best a faint smudge.
card.deeper: Reyes-Pérez et al. (2015) modeled the WN6 star and NGC 6888 together and found a stellar temperature of about 70,000 K best fits both; star and nebula are nitrogen-rich and oxygen-poor, the chemical fingerprint of material processed in the star. Rubio et al. (2020) modeled the infrared dust: the nebula holds about 25.5 (+4.7/−2.8) solar masses of gas, mostly ejected by WR 136 itself, implying an initial mass of up to about 50 Suns. Gaia EDR3 gives 0.577 ± 0.016 mas (about 5,650 ly).

historyHook.text: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel caught 61 Cygni shifting slightly against the background as Earth orbited the Sun: the first measured distance to a star.

card.question: Which star first showed how far away the stars really are?
card.glance: A faint naked-eye star south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.whyHere: For centuries nobody knew whether the stars lay just beyond the planets or unimaginably far, and this faint orange pair in Cygnus settled it.
card.see: Find 61 Cygni about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart, a lovely contrast with white Deneb, which lies well over a hundred times farther away.
card.understand: As Earth swings around the Sun, a nearby star shifts very slightly against the distant ones behind it, just as your thumb jumps when you close one eye and then the other. Friedrich Bessel picked 61 Cygni because it crept across the sky unusually fast, a hint that it was close, and in 1838 he caught that tiny yearly shift. The angle was about a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from across a city.
card.wonder: It moves about 5 arcseconds a year, enough to cross a full Moon's width in roughly 350 years.
card.connect: Barnard's Star in Ophiuchus moves twice as fast, the sky's speed record.
card.answer: 61 Cygni, about 11 light-years away. Turning that small angle into a distance showed for the first time that even a nearby star is so remote that its light takes over a decade to reach us.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows the pair 32″ apart; over decades both stars visibly shift together against the background.
card.deeper: Bessel (1838) chose 61 Cyg because of its large proper motion and measured a parallax of about 0.3″ with a heliometer. Gaia EDR3 gives 285.995 ± 0.060 mas (11.40 ly) and a proper motion of about 5.28″ per year. The WDS lists the pair STF 2758 AB at 32.0″, PA 154° (2025); the stars are a bound K5 V + K7 V binary. "Light-year" is a distance, not a time.

the closest single star to the Sun
superlatives.scope: whole sky (only the α Centauri system is closer)

historyHook.text: E. E. Barnard reported its record-breaking motion in 1916; in 2024–25 astronomers finally confirmed four small planets around it.

images.caption: Artist's impression of the planet Barnard b; an illustration, not a photograph.

card.question: Why can't you see one of the Sun's nearest neighbors with the naked eye?
card.glance: A faint 9½-magnitude red-orange speck about 2° north-north-west of 67 Ophiuchi; chart and dark sky essential.
card.whyHere: If the nearest stars had to be the brightest, Barnard's Star would break the rule: only 6 light-years away, it is invisible without optics.
card.see: Hop with the chart from Cebalrai (β Oph) in Ophiuchus about 4° east to 67 Oph, then 2° north-north-west to a dim point with a faint orange cast. Sketch the field and come back in a few years, because it visibly shifts against its neighbors.
card.understand: Barnard's Star is a red dwarf, a star much smaller than the Sun with a surface near 3,200 K. A star's output climbs steeply with both size and temperature, so this one gives off only a tiny fraction of the Sun's light. In 1916 E. E. Barnard noticed that it crawls across the sky faster than any other star, the giveaway that it is close, since distant stars barely seem to move.
card.wonder: It crosses a full Moon's width in under two centuries, and in 2024–25 astronomers confirmed at least four small planets riding along with it.
card.connect: η Aquilae looks far brighter yet lies over a hundred times farther away.
card.answer: Because most stars are not like the Sun. The commonest kind is a dim red dwarf like this one, too feeble for the eye even at 6 light-years, and the bright stars of the night sky are rare, powerful ones seen from much farther off.
card.photoCaption: The ESO image is an artist's impression of a planet; no telescope has photographed the planets themselves.
card.notSee: Its planets are known only from tiny wobbles in the star's motion.
card.deeper: Barnard (1916) reported its motion of about 10.3″ per year; Gaia EDR3 gives 10.39″/yr and a parallax of 546.976 ± 0.040 mas (5.96 ly). Because it moves so fast, the app propagates its position from J2000. ESO's ESPRESSO team announced planet b (period 3.15 d, at least half the mass of Venus) in 2024; Basant et al. (2025) confirmed b and three more sub-Earths (periods 2.34, 4.12 and 6.74 d; 0.19–0.34 Earth masses).

teffK.note: median of 21 SIMBAD Teff entries; it changes through the pulsation cycle

superlatives.claim: one of the brightest Cepheid variables in the sky

card.question: How can a star's steady pulse reveal how far away it is?
card.glance: A naked-eye star in the eagle, Aquila, whose brightness rises and falls over a week.
card.whyHere: Distances are the hardest numbers in astronomy, and η Aquilae helped make them measurable by beating like a clock whose rhythm gives away its true power.
card.see: η Aquilae sits about 8° south of Altair, in a line with δ and θ Aquilae. At its brightest it nearly matches δ Aql, and at its faintest it sinks to about ι Aql, so a log of brighter-than and fainter-than shows the whole cycle within a week or two.
card.understand: η Aquilae is a Cepheid, a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 7.2 days. Below the surface lies a layer of helium that turns more opaque when squeezed, trapping heat like a lid on a pot until the pressure lifts it, then letting the heat out and falling back. Henrietta Leavitt discovered that slower Cepheids are truly more luminous, so the rhythm announces the star's real power.
card.wonder: Gaia measured its distance directly, about 888 light-years, which is exactly what a cosmic ruler needs as its anchor.
card.connect: RR Lyrae, old and light, beats nearly twice a day as the summer sky's other yardstick.
card.answer: Compare that real power with how bright the star looks, and the shortfall tells you how far its light has traveled. The same rule, applied to Cepheids in other galaxies, first proved that those galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visual shows the classic quick-rise, slow-fall Cepheid light curve.
card.deeper: VSX gives V = 3.49–4.30 and P = 7.17679 d (type DCEP); the spectrum swings between about F6 Iab and G4 Ib as the surface heats and cools. Gaia EDR3 measures 3.67 ± 0.19 mas (about 890 ly). The period–luminosity relation (Leavitt's law) is calibrated with nearby Cepheids like this one and then applied to Cepheids in other galaxies. SIMBAD temperature measurements range from about 4,800 to 6,200 K depending on phase.

card.question: What becomes of a middle-weight star when its core runs out of hydrogen?
card.glance: An orange-red star marking the head of Hercules, 5° west of white Rasalhague: two heads side by side.
card.whyHere: Stars change most dramatically near the end, and Rasalgethi shows that stage up close, a giant so swollen and cool that its surface heaves like a slow sea.
card.see: Rasalgethi and Rasalhague, the heads of Hercules and Ophiuchus, sit about 5° apart and fit in one low-power sweep, one orange-red and one white. Over weeks Rasalgethi's brightness wanders, sometimes drawing much closer to its neighbor's, and its 5th-magnitude companion is too close for binoculars.
card.understand: Once the hydrogen in a star's core runs out, the core shrinks and heats while the outer layers balloon outward and cool. Interferometers measure Rasalgethi's disk at 36 thousandths of an arcsecond across, and at its distance that means a star hundreds of times wider than the Sun. Its loose outer layers heave irregularly, so its light drifts, while a slow wind carries them away.
card.wonder: If Rasalgethi replaced the Sun, Earth would be orbiting inside the star.
card.connect: Rasalhague, 5° away, is a hot white star at the other end of the color scale.
card.answer: A red giant like Rasalgethi: hundreds of times wider than the Sun, cool enough to glow orange-red, and slowly giving its outer layers back to space.
card.photoCaption: The survey photo shows only a saturated star; the color is best judged by eye.
card.notSee: The bluish-green-looking companion α² Her, 4.9″ away, needs a small telescope.
card.deeper: VSX classifies α Her A as a semiregular variable (SRB) ranging V 2.73–3.60 with a characteristic timescale of about 126 days; GCVS lists it as SRC with 2.74–4.0. Hipparcos 2007 gives 9.07 ± 1.32 mas (about 360 ly, ±15%). The WDS lists the AB pair (STF 2140) at 4.9″. Mark III interferometry measured a limb-darkened diameter of 36.0 ± 0.4 mas (Mozurkewich et al. 2003); at the Hipparcos distance that is roughly 370–500 solar radii, so the uncertainty is mostly the distance.

superlatives.claim: one of the first stars known to host a planet on a highly stretched orbit

historyHook.text: In 1996 a planet at least 1.5 times Jupiter's mass was found swinging around it on a 2.2-year, highly elongated orbit.

card.question: What would our Sun be like with a twin beside it?
card.glance: One of a matched pair of 6th-magnitude yellowish stars 40″ apart, on the swan's western wing in Cygnus.
card.whyHere: Planet hunting began with stars like the Sun, and 16 Cygni is the summer sky's best test: two Sun-like stars born together, only one with a known giant planet.
card.see: From δ Cygni, go about 5° north with the chart to a pair of equal faint stars 40″ apart, split at 10× on a steady mount. Both share a soft yellow-white tint, and 16 Cyg B is the slightly fainter one, to the south-east.
card.understand: Both stars are close copies of the Sun in temperature and mass. Stars ring like bells, and since the tones depend on what is inside, the Kepler spacecraft's measurements of their tiny pulsations gave both an age of about 6.8 billion years, older than the Sun. In 1996 astronomers found a planet at least 1.5 times Jupiter's mass circling B once every 2.2 years on a strongly stretched orbit.
card.wonder: From that planet, 16 Cygni A would shine as a brilliant second sun.
card.connect: HD 189733, near the Dumbbell Nebula, has a planet whose color has been measured.
card.answer: It would look much like 16 Cygni, two near-identical suns sharing a long, wide orbit and tugging on each other's planets. B's giant may owe its wildly stretched path to its sibling, a hint that our own calm, round orbits are a privilege of a single star.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visuals compare it with the Sun.
card.notSee: The planet 16 Cyg Bb is far too faint and too close to its star to see; it was found from the star's wobble.
card.deeper: Cochran et al. (1997) found 16 Cyg Bb from radial velocities: P = 800.8 d, m sin i = 1.5 Jupiter masses, e = 0.63 (the NASA Exoplanet Archive now lists 798.5 d and e = 0.68). Metcalfe et al. (2012) modeled 46 and 41 oscillation frequencies from Kepler data and obtained a common age of 6.8 ± 0.4 Gyr. The WDS lists the pair at 40.0″; A also has a faint M-dwarf companion 3.3″ away. Both components have Gaia EDR3 parallaxes of 47.33 mas (69 ly).

superlatives.claim: host of the first exoplanet whose color was measured (deep blue)

historyHook.text: In 2013 Hubble measured its planet's color by catching the dip in blue light as the planet slipped behind the star: a deep azure world.

images.caption: Artist's impression of the blue planet HD 189733b; an illustration, not a photograph.

card.question: How do astronomers study a planet they can never actually see?
card.glance: A 7½-magnitude star a quarter of a degree from the Dumbbell Nebula in Vulpecula; both fit in one binocular field.
card.whyHere: Most known planets have never been seen directly, and this ordinary orange star shows how astronomers learn about them anyway.
card.see: Center the Dumbbell Nebula, M27, in little Vulpecula just north of Sagitta, the Arrow. HD 189733 is the brighter star about half a Moon-width away; when its planet crosses in front, the star dims by only about 3%, far too little for the eye.
card.understand: The planet is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant a little heavier than Jupiter that circles its star in just over two days. Its orbit is edge-on to us, so every lap it crosses the star's face, and the depth of the dip gives its size. When it slips behind the star the light dips again by a whisker, and in 2013 Hubble noticed that this second dip happened only in blue light.
card.wonder: The star is about 20 times closer than the Dumbbell Nebula beside it, so the two share a binocular field and nothing else.
card.connect: The Dumbbell in the same field is the shell of a dying star, far in the background.
card.answer: Everything comes from the starlight: transits give the planet's size, starlight filtering through its air reveals its atmosphere, and the blue-only eclipse gave away its color. HD 189733 b is a deep azure world, tinted probably by a haze of silicate grains, tiny particles of glass.
card.photoCaption: The ESA/Hubble image is an artist's impression of the planet; no image of the planet itself exists.
card.notSee: The planet and its 3% transits; the color was measured from a one-part-in-ten-thousand dip in blue light.
card.deeper: Bouchy et al. (2005) discovered the transiting planet with ELODIE: 1.15 ± 0.04 Jupiter masses, 1.26 ± 0.03 Jupiter radii, a 2.219-day orbit and a transit depth of about 3%. Hubble/STIS observed the system as the planet passed behind the star and found a drop only in blue light, implying a deep blue planet (ESA/Hubble heic1312), probably from silicate haze. Gaia EDR3 gives 50.57 mas (64.5 ly). The angular offset from M27 (0.26°) is computed from catalog positions; the "20 times" comparison assumes the Dumbbell's commonly quoted distance of over a thousand light-years and should be checked against the deep-sky record.

superlatives.claim: the star that revealed the aberration of starlight, proof that Earth moves

historyHook.text: Trying to measure its distance in the 1720s, James Bradley instead found that starlight arrives at a slight angle because Earth is moving: the first direct proof of Earth's orbit.

card.question: Which star proved that the Earth really moves around the Sun?
card.glance: The brightest star in the dragon's head, a lopsided quadrangle about 14° north-west of Vega; orange in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Some stars matter for what they are and some for what they let us measure, and Eltanin, an ordinary orange giant, gave the first direct proof that Earth is moving.
card.see: From Vega, look about 14° north-west for the four-star head of Draco. Eltanin is the brightest of the four, at the head's southern corner beside Rastaban, and in binoculars it is clearly orange while Rastaban looks yellower.
card.understand: In the 1720s James Bradley set out to measure Eltanin's parallax, choosing it because it passed almost straight overhead in London. He did find a yearly shift, but it was far too large and peaked at the wrong times of year to be parallax. The explanation is one you meet driving through rain: falling drops seem to slant toward the windshield because the car is moving, and starlight arriving at a moving Earth slants the same way.
card.wonder: The light you see left Eltanin about 150 years ago, in the age of steam trains.
card.connect: A century later, 61 Cygni gave the first measured distance to a star.
card.answer: Eltanin, though the star itself did nothing. The slant of its light swung back and forth over the year exactly as Earth's orbital motion predicted, and from the size of the slant Bradley could even estimate the speed of light.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; the visuals compare its color and size with the Sun.
card.deeper: Bradley announced the aberration of light in 1729 (Phil. Trans. 35, 637), from zenith-sector observations of γ Draconis made at Kew and Wanstead from 1725. The yearly displacement of about 20″ arises from Earth's orbital speed relative to the speed of light. He was searching for parallax, which is far smaller (Hipparcos: 21.14 ± 0.10 mas, about 154 ly). card.question: Why does this faint star beside Vega glow as red as blood?
card.glance: A faint, distinctly red dot about 2° south-west of Vega: one binocular field holds a blue-white star and one of the reddest.
card.whyHere: Much of the carbon in the universe was made inside stars, and T Lyrae is one of the factories, caught in the act.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 2° south-west. T Lyrae is a faint star with a strong red tint, easiest at 10× under dark skies; glance from it to Vega and back rather than staring, since red stars seem to brighten under a steady gaze.
card.understand: Late in life some giants dredge carbon up from the furnace in their cores to the surface, becoming carbon stars. In the cool atmosphere that carbon forms molecules and soot, which absorb blue and green light much as smoke reddens a sunset. Measured through blue and yellow filters, T Lyrae comes out redder than almost anything else in binocular range.
card.wonder: Its winds are seeding the Galaxy with carbon dust that will end up in new stars and planets.
card.connect: Vega, in the same field, is blue-white from heat alone.
card.answer: Its color is mostly a filter rather than a temperature: carbon in its atmosphere strips out the blue, leaving a deep red glow. Some of the carbon in your own body was made in stars like this and blown into space long before the Sun formed.

card.deeper: SIMBAD classifies T Lyr as C-J4: p, a "J-type" carbon star rich in carbon-13. VSX lists an irregular (LB) range of V 7.5–9.2. Its B−V of about 4.9 (from single-epoch SIMBAD photometry) is extreme; the color comes mostly from molecular absorption rather than a very low temperature. Gaia EDR3 gives 2.321 ± 0.036 mas, but parallax errors for bright AGB stars are known to be underestimated, so the range here is widened.

card.question: Why is the sky around Sadr so crowded with stars?
card.glance: The star at the crossing of the Northern Cross in Cygnus, swarmed in binoculars by faint Milky Way stars.
card.whyHere: Every star tonight belongs to one flat disk, the Milky Way, and at Sadr you are looking straight along it, which changes the view completely.
card.see: Center Sadr and sweep slowly. Dozens of faint stars crowd every field with dark patches between them, and under a dark sky the whole region glows, split by the dark lanes of the Cygnus Rift.
card.understand: Our Galaxy is a flat disk of stars, so the number you see depends on where you look: out of the disk you see through a thin layer, but along it you look through thousands of light-years of stars stacked behind one another. In Cygnus the line of sight runs along the disk, so the faint background piles up. Sadr itself is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star grown huge and bright, about 1,800 light-years away and only a little hotter than the Sun.
card.wonder: The light reaching you from Sadr set out while the Roman Empire still ruled the Mediterranean.
card.connect: Hidden in this crowd is P Cygni, a star that blazed up in 1600.
card.answer: You are looking down the long axis of a flat crowd. Even the dark lanes that break it up are part of it: not empty space but dust in the disk, blocking the stars behind.
card.photoCaption: No photo is bundled; long exposures of this region show red glowing gas (IC 1318) that binoculars do not show.
card.notSee: The red emission nebulae around Sadr are photographic; the eye sees at most a faint glow.
card.deeper: Hipparcos 2007 gives 1.78 ± 0.27 mas (about 1,800 ly, ±15%). SIMBAD Teff measurements cluster near 6,000 K, consistent with its F8 Ib type. The glowing gas photographed around it is cataloged as IC 1318. The statement that most of the surrounding field stars are more distant is a general property of Milky Way star clouds, not a measured statistic for this field.

card.question: Is the Northern Crown's brightest jewel really a single star?

card.understand: Watched with sensitive instruments, its light dips slightly every 17 days. The dips come from two stars, a hot white one and a smaller Sun-like one, taking turns to pass in front of each other. We notice only because our line of sight lies almost in the plane of their orbit.

card.answer: Alphecca is an eclipsing pair whose dips are far too small for the eye, so its steady look hides a rhythm only instruments can catch.

card.question: Can binoculars show you a star with its own family of planets?
card.glance: A 5th-magnitude yellowish star about 6° north of ε CrB, beyond the open side of the Northern Crown; easy in binoculars.
card.whyHere: Planets around other suns sound remote, but some of their stars are easy binocular targets, and ρ Coronae Borealis is one of the friendliest.
card.see: Sweep north from ε CrB with the chart to a plain yellow-white point about 6° away. Nothing marks it out in the field; the interest lies in what circles it.
card.understand: A planet tugs its star as it orbits, so the star wobbles toward us and away. That motion shifts the dark lines in its spectrum by a tiny, measurable amount. Watching ρ CrB this way has revealed a Jupiter-mass world on a 40-day orbit and smaller ones beyond it.
card.wonder: It is somewhat poorer in heavy elements than the Sun, yet it still built planets.
card.connect: 14 Herculis, nearby, holds giant planets on wide orbits instead.
card.answer: ρ CrB is one, an easy binocular star 57 light-years away with at least three planets, each found from the wobble it causes.

card.question: What does a planetary system with giant outer planets look like?

card.connect: ρ Coronae Borealis, nearby, keeps its biggest planet close to the star instead.
card.answer: Much like 14 Herculis, with giants several times Jupiter's mass on slow, wide orbits around a star well stocked with planet-building material.

card.question: How steady do your binoculars need to be to split a close pair?

card.wonder: Splitting it trains the same skill as Albireo, with a tighter gap.
card.connect: The wide doubles of Draco and Lyra make an easy comparison.
card.answer: Steady enough to hold 10× still: braced, 10× binoculars split the 27″ gap, while hand-held 7× shows only a stretched star.

card.question: How cool can a star's surface be and still shine?

card.understand: g Herculis is an old giant about 240 times wider than the Sun. Its thin, cool outer layers pulse roughly every three months, slowly leaking into space. Stars this cool glow mostly in infrared, so the eye catches only the red tail of their light.
card.wonder: Its pulses are a sign of old age: stars only start to breathe like this when their cores are nearly spent.

card.question: What will the Sun look like when it grows old?

card.wonder: When the Sun reaches this stage, its swollen disk will fill a broad patch of Earth's sky.
card.connect: Red Rasalgethi shows a giant at a later, puffier stage.
card.answer: In several billion years, once its core hydrogen runs out, the Sun should swell into a yellow giant much like Kornephoros.

card.question: What happens as a star like the Sun begins to age?
card.glance: The south-western corner of the Keystone of Hercules, a pale yellow star 35 light-years away.

card.wonder: Its light took about 35 years to reach you, so it left around the time many of today's parents were children.
card.connect: The Great Hercules Cluster, next door, is a city of far older stars.
card.answer: It begins to swell, as ζ Herculis is doing now on its way to becoming a giant.

card.question: Can two stars side by side show both ends of the color scale?

card.question: Which orange star points the way to Barnard's Star?

card.answer: Cebalrai, an orange giant whose bright glow makes it the ideal guide; Barnard's Star lies about 3½° to its east.

card.question: What do the Sun's nearest naked-eye neighbors look like?
card.glance: A 4th-magnitude orange star in Ophiuchus, about 3° from Barnard's Star: one of the Sun's nearest naked-eye neighbors.
card.whyHere: Near Barnard's Star sits a neighbor you can see without optics, and it shows what a close star looks like when it is not a red dwarf.
card.see: Binoculars show 70 Ophiuchi as a single warm orange point about 3° from Barnard's Star. Its companion is only 7″ away and needs a telescope.
card.understand: 70 Ophiuchi is two orange dwarfs, stars a little smaller and cooler than the Sun, circling each other. Astronomers have followed the pair around its orbit for well over a century. Timing that orbit, together with the distance, gives the mass of each star, which is how we weigh stars without touching them.
card.wonder: From a planet there, the Sun would be just one more modest star in the sky.
card.connect: Barnard's Star, its neighbor on the sky, is even closer but much fainter.
card.answer: They look like 70 Ophiuchi, a warm orange glow that is really two orange dwarfs, under 17 light-years away, swinging around each other.

card.question: How close can two stars be before binoculars merge them into one?
card.glance: Two identical white 6th-magnitude stars only 14″ apart in Hercules: the hardest common binocular split.
card.whyHere: After the easy doubles comes the real test, and 100 Herculis sits right at the edge of what binoculars can do.
card.see: Mount or brace 10× binoculars and focus with care: at best you will see two touching white points. At 7× expect a single, slightly stretched star, and that tells you something too.
card.understand: Every lens spreads a star into a tiny blur, and two stars split only when their blurs stop overlapping. Magnification enlarges the gap, while a steady mount stops the blurs from smearing together. Because these two stars are nearly equal, neither drowns the other, which makes them a fair test.
card.wonder: Their light left them about two centuries ago, so you are testing your optics on twins seen as they were then.
card.connect: Wider pairs elsewhere in the summer sky make the contrast clear.
card.answer: These two mark the limit: at 14″ apart, braced 10× binoculars show two touching points, while at 7× the pair merges.

card.question: Why are so many bright stars yellow or orange giants?

card.question: Is this easy pair in Draco really a family?

card.question: Is there a binocular double that never sets?

card.question: Can you see a star's temperature by comparing two neighbors?
card.glance: An orange-red 4th-magnitude star at the north-east corner of Lyra's parallelogram, with blue-white δ¹ nearby.
card.whyHere: The cleanest way to read temperature is side by side, and δ Lyrae puts a cool giant and a hot star in one binocular field.
card.see: About 3½° north of Sheliak, δ² Lyrae glows orange-red, with fainter blue-white δ¹ about a third of a Moon-width to the west. Defocus slightly and the colors deepen.
card.understand: δ² is a cool bright giant about 290 times wider than the Sun, with a surface near 3,500 K. δ¹ is a hot blue star, many times hotter. Your eye compares them under the same sky and through the same air, so any difference in tint belongs to the stars.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 770 years ago, while Europe’s great Gothic cathedrals were rising.
card.connect: Sheliak, at the parallelogram's far corner, is a pair of stars that swap gas.
card.answer: You can: cool δ² glows orange-red and hot δ¹ blue-white, a temperature gap your eye reads at a glance.

card.question: What turns a dying star a deep orange-red?
card.glance: A 7th-magnitude, strikingly red star less than 1° south-west of λ Aquilae, in southern Aquila.
card.whyHere: Carbon is the backbone of life, and V Aquilae is one of the places it is made, glowing red with the evidence.
card.see: From λ Aquilae in southern Aquila, move about 1° south-west. V Aql is the obviously red point in the field, and the color is clearest when you compare it with any white star nearby.
card.understand: V Aquilae is a carbon star, a dying giant that has dredged carbon from its core up to its surface. In the cool atmosphere that carbon forms molecules that absorb blue light, so the star looks redder than its temperature alone would make it. It also pulses gently, over about 407 days.
card.wonder: The carbon it makes will drift into space and end up in future planets.
card.connect: Its cousin T Lyrae waits beside Vega.
card.answer: The more carbon a dying giant dredges up, the more blue light its atmosphere swallows, and V Aquilae has dredged up a lot.

card.question: How can astronomers tell that a star is spinning fast?
card.glance: A white 3rd-magnitude star marking the eagle's tail in Aquila, about 12° west-north-west of Altair.
card.whyHere: You cannot watch a star turn, but its light records the spin, and Deneb el Okab is a fine example.
card.see: Deneb el Okab is a clean white point about 12° west-north-west of Altair, at the eagle's tail. Compare it with orange Tarazed for a quick color lesson.
card.understand: Spread a star's light into a rainbow and you find dark lines at particular colors. When a star spins, one edge rushes toward us and its light shifts bluer, while the other rushes away and shifts redder. Each line gets smeared out, and the wider the smear, the faster the spin.
card.wonder: The same smearing in Altair's light was an early clue that it spins fast enough to change its shape.
card.connect: Altair shows what fast spin does to a star's shape.
card.answer: Deneb el Okab's spectral lines are smeared very wide, because one side of the star approaches while the other recedes, the mark of fast rotation.

card.question: What might the Sun look like a couple of billion years from now?
card.glance: The slightly brighter of the matched 16 Cygni pair, 40″ from its twin, about 5° north of δ Cygni.
card.whyHere: 16 Cygni A is the planet-less twin of the pair, and that makes it simply the best preview of an older Sun.
card.see: Split the 16 Cygni pair at 10× on a steady mount and compare two equal yellow-white points. A is the one to the north-west of B.
card.understand: Kepler measured its starquakes, tiny ripples across the surface, and the way they travel through the star revealed its age, about 6.8 billion years. That makes it a couple of billion years older than the Sun, yet it still shines steadily. A faint red-dwarf companion orbits it 3″ away, far beyond binocular reach.
card.wonder: Its twin, born from the same cloud, has a giant planet; whether A ever had one is unknown.
card.connect: Its sibling 16 Cyg B carries the planet.
card.answer: Much like 16 Cygni A: a Sun-like star in late middle age, still steady and a little brighter than in its youth.

card.question: Is Altair's orange neighbor really its neighbor?
card.glance: The orange star 2° north-north-west of Altair in Aquila; the color contrast in binoculars is obvious.
card.whyHere: Stars that look like a set often are not, and Tarazed beside Altair is one of the clearest cases.
card.see: Put Altair and Tarazed in one field: crisp white against warm orange, about 2° apart. They look like a matched set, which makes the truth more surprising.
card.understand: Tarazed is a bright giant about 95 times wider than the Sun, some 400 light-years away. Altair is a modest star only 17 light-years off. Seen from the side, the two would be nowhere near each other; they merely line up from where we stand.
card.wonder: Their light set out at very different times: Altair's about 17 years ago, Tarazed's around four centuries ago.
card.connect: Albireo, by contrast, is a pair whose two stars really do lie at about the same distance.
card.answer: Tarazed lies more than 20 times farther away than Altair and only looks comparable because it is a giant.

card.question: Which star leads you to the 16 Cygni twins?
card.glance: The white star at the end of the Northern Cross's western arm in Cygnus, 8° north-west of Sadr.
card.whyHere: Good hops start from stars you can't miss, and Al Fawaris is the stepping stone to two Sun-like twins.
card.see: Al Fawaris is a bright white point at the end of the Northern Cross's western arm. From it, the 16 Cygni pair lies about 5° to the north, an easy sweep with a chart.
card.understand: Al Fawaris is a hot white star about 165 light-years away. With a surface near 10,000 K it is nearly twice as hot as the Sun, which is why it looks white rather than yellow. It is a little past the start of its long steady phase, still young as stars go.
card.wonder: From a planet circling Al Fawaris, our Sun would be too faint to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Two Sun-like twins lie a short hop north.
card.answer: Al Fawaris, at the tip of the Cross's western arm: from there the 16 Cygni twins lie about 5° north.

card.question: Can binoculars show Albireo's colors with an easier split?
card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue-white companion: a binocular color group with 30 Cygni.
card.whyHere: Albireo's gold-and-blue lesson can be hard to split, and 31 Cygni repeats it with room to spare, plus a secret of its own.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter star closer in. The gaps are wider than Albireo's, so the colors come easily.
card.understand: 31 Cygni is an orange supergiant, a cool star swollen to huge size. A hot blue star orbits it and slips behind it every 10.4 years. As the blue star sinks, its light shines for a while through the giant's thin outer atmosphere, so astronomers can probe that air like a lamp seen through fog.
card.wonder: The orange star is about 160 times wider than the Sun, so its closest partner, a hot star far too close to split, takes weeks to slip behind it at each eclipse.
card.connect: Albireo shows the same colors at a tighter split.
card.answer: 31 Cygni does, pairing an orange supergiant with blue-white neighbors set wide enough for any binoculars.

card.question: What color is the star at the corner of the Dolphin?
card.glance: The golden star at the north-east corner of the little diamond of Delphinus, Job's Coffin.
card.whyHere: Delphinus is a tiny constellation that binoculars frame perfectly, and its corner star rewards a closer look at color.
card.see: Frame the whole dolphin in one field; γ Del is the warm-tinted star at the far corner of the diamond. Its 9″ companion is a telescope target, but the tint is plain in binoculars.
card.understand: γ Delphini is a subgiant, a star just starting to swell with age, which has cooled to an orange glow near 4,800 K. Its companion is a yellow-white star a little warmer than the Sun. Small telescopes split them, and the color pair is a favorite of double-star observers.
card.wonder: Its light left about 116 years ago, a few years after the Wright brothers first flew.
card.connect: Albireo and 31 Cygni are color pairs you can split in binoculars.
card.answer: It glows golden-orange, an aging star with a yellow-white partner too close for binoculars.

card.question: Which star points the way to the Veil Nebula?
card.glance: The orange star at the tip of the swan's eastern wing in Cygnus, about 8° south-east of Sadr.
card.whyHere: Aljanah is an easy orange giant in its own right, and the signpost to the wreck of a star that exploded.
card.see: Aljanah is a clear orange-yellow point at the swan's eastern wingtip. The faint arcs of the Veil lie about 3° to the south-east, and you need dark skies and ideally a nebula filter to find them.
card.understand: Aljanah is a giant about 11 times wider than the Sun, 73 light-years away, that has finished burning hydrogen in its core. Its tint comes from a surface near 4,750 K, cooler than the Sun's. An interferometer measured its tiny disk, so its size is a measurement rather than a guess.
card.wonder: The Veil beyond it is the debris of a star that exploded thousands of years ago.
card.connect: The supernova wreckage is one short hop away.
card.answer: Aljanah, the swan's eastern wingtip: the Veil's arcs lie about 3° to its south-east.

card.question: Which red giant can you watch pulse over a single season?
card.glance: A reddish 5th–7th-magnitude star less than half a degree south-east of ρ Cygni.
card.whyHere: χ Cygni's swings are spectacular but slow, while W Cygni pulses faster and stays within binocular reach, so you can follow a whole cycle.
card.see: Center ρ Cygni; W Cyg is the reddish star just to its south-east. Compare it with ρ Cyg each week over a season and you will see it rise and fall.
card.understand: W Cygni is a cool red giant late in life, swelling and shrinking roughly every 130 days. As it pulses its brightness changes about fivefold, and each cycle pushes a little more gas into space. Its rhythm is looser than a Cepheid's, so no two cycles look quite the same.
card.wonder: Set in the Sun's place, its surface would reach about as far as Earth's orbit.
card.connect: χ Cygni swings far more extremely.
card.answer: Watch W Cygni beside ρ Cygni through the summer and you will see one or two full breaths of a dying giant.

card.question: Where is the brightest carbon star of the northern summer sky?
card.glance: A 6th-magnitude orange-red star in eastern Cygnus, about 6° east-south-east of τ Cygni.
card.whyHere: Carbon stars are rare and often faint, but V460 Cygni is bright enough to spot with almost any binoculars.
card.see: Use the chart from τ Cygni, about 6° to the west-north-west; V460 Cyg stands out by its warm orange-red tint among white field stars. Glance between it and a white star nearby, and the tint becomes obvious.
card.understand: V460 Cygni is a carbon star, a dying giant that has dredged carbon from its core to its surface. There the carbon forms molecules that absorb blue light and redden its glow. Its gentle brightness changes take about half a year.
card.wonder: It lies about 1,900 light-years away, so the light you see left it in Roman times.
card.connect: T Lyrae and V Aquilae are redder cousins.
card.answer: It lies in eastern Cygnus, where V460 Cygni shines as an easy 6th-magnitude carbon star, reddened by the carbon it has brought to its surface.

card.question: Do light and heavy stars shed their skins the same way?
card.glance: A red carbon star half a degree north-east of WR 136, in the rich field south-west of Sadr.
card.whyHere: In one binocular field near Sadr sit two stars giving their outer layers back to space, in completely different styles.
card.see: Center WR 136, then look about 0.45° north-east: RS Cyg is the reddish point. Near minimum it may sink below easy binocular reach.
card.understand: RS Cygni is a cool, carbon-rich giant, pulsing on a cycle of about 14 months and losing gas in a slow wind. That wind is gentle and cool, and dust forms in it as it drifts outward. WR 136, its neighbor on the sky, is a stripped heavyweight blasting its gas out in a fast, scorching gale.
card.wonder: Whatever the speed, both winds will end up seeding new stars.
card.connect: The Crescent Nebula around WR 136 shows where a heavy star's gale ends up.
card.answer: A light star like RS Cygni leaks gas in a slow, cool breeze, while a heavy one like WR 136 blows it away in a fast, hot wind.

card.question: Why does this hidden star flare up every month or two?
card.glance: Invisible in binoculars most of the time; every month or two it flares to about 8th magnitude for a few days.
card.whyHere: T Coronae Borealis saves up for one explosion a lifetime; SS Cygni runs a smaller version of the same arrangement on fast-forward.
card.see: Find the spot with the chart, about 2½° south-east of ρ Cygni. Usually there is nothing to see, but in outburst a new 8th-magnitude point appears for several days.
card.understand: Gas from an orange dwarf spirals into a disk around a white dwarf, the Earth-sized remnant of a star. The disk fills slowly until it turns unstable, heats up all at once and dumps its gas inward. Unlike T CrB, there is no nuclear blast, just a disk suddenly blazing.
card.wonder: The two stars whirl around each other in under seven hours.
card.connect: T CrB stores fuel for a far bigger blast on its white dwarf's surface.
card.answer: Its disk fills and bursts like a dam: every month or two it heats up and the system brightens about seventy-fold.
